prompt: A small team wants to write its own login, password reset and two-factor auth instead of using an established auth service.
tells: write its own login, password reset and two-factor auth
why: Solved problems that aren't your edge are usually better bought.
trap: It's not about a new tool; it's whether to write it at all.

prompt: A logistics startup writes its own route-planning engine because that's what customers pay them for, but uses a hosted service for email.
tells: because that's what customers pay them for
why: Build the differentiator; buy the commodity.
trap: Both halves together show the build-or-buy split.

prompt: An engineer starts writing time-zone conversion code by hand. A reviewer points to a well-maintained library that already handles it.
tells: points to a well-maintained library that already handles it
why: Don't rebuild what a mature library already does.
trap: The library is proven, but the choice is write it or use it.

prompt: The search vendor now costs more than two engineers a year and limits a feature customers want. The team weighs building search in-house.
tells: costs more than two engineers a year and limits a feature customers want
why: Revisit buy-or-build as costs and needs change.
trap: It may be hard to undo, but the question is build or buy.

prompt: Comparing options, the lead counts not just the time to write a scheduler but years of on-call, upgrades and bug fixes.
tells: years of on-call, upgrades and bug fixes
why: Owning code includes maintaining it forever.
trap: It's a cost comparison of making vs using.

prompt: In a behavioral interview, a candidate explains how they convinced their team to use an open-source job queue instead of finishing their half-built one.
tells: use an open-source job queue instead of finishing their half-built one
why: Use what exists when it does the job.
trap: They persuaded people, but the decision was build or buy.
